newsitem.title: USA: US Airways expected to keep Shuttle.
newsitem.headline: US Airways expected to keep Shuttle.

text.p: American Airlines moved Thursday to buy the US Airways Shuttle, a commuter airline serving New York, Washington and Boston, but US Airways, which operates the service, was expected to rebuff the bid.

In an attempt to strengthen its position in the lucrative northeast corridor, American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., said it reached a binding agreement to buy the stock, warrants and debt of Shuttle Inc. from the investment group that owns it for an undisclosed price.

However, the agreement is contingent upon US Airways' decision not to exercise its option to purchase the Shuttle or its right to match American's offer, and airline industry analysts said they doubt US Airways will let the shuttle go without a fight.

"It's pretty clear that US Airways wants it. What's held them up is their labour situation. US Airways knows better than anyone what the Shuttle's worth. When all is said and done, 'Will US Airways get the Shuttle?' I think 'Yes,'" said Edward Starkman, an analyst with Dillon Read.
US Airways said it has "exclusive contract rights" to buy the Shuttle and it is working with the banks that partly own the service "to determine how we will proceed."

"It's a very complicated process and may take a very long time to sort out. It's not at all certain that American will emerge as the victor," said Candace Browning, an airline analyst with Merrill Lynch.
The Shuttle is seen as a crucial piece of US Airways' plan to create a low-cost unit to compete with rivals such as Southwest Airlines Co. and Delta Air Lines Inc.'s Delta Express unit.

US Airways' plans have stalled since it has not yet reached a cost-cutting pact with its unionized employees. As part of its labour talks, the airline and its pilots are debating the size and format of the proposed low-cost unit and pay scales for its employees.
US Airways operates the shuttle, the successor to the Trump Shuttle, under a management contract and holds 47 percent of the equity.
American's bid to buy the Shuttle now adds more pressure to US Airways' already contentious labour talks, analysts said.
"There are so many pressure points in that situation that it's hard to weigh them. But it certainly adds to it," said Dillon Read's Starkman.
US Airways' pilots declined to comment on how American's offer to buy the Shuttle would effect negotiations.

Although the shuttle is a small property, it is an attractive acquisition target and would give American a strong foothold in the East Coast's frequent-flyer business market, Browning said. "It's a clever move for American," she said.
American will said it will receive a break-up fee if the deal is not completed. The airline declined to disclose the amount of the fee.
American said the Shuttle will supplement its current presence on the East Coast, but said it has not yet decided whether it will expand the Shuttle beyond its existing operations.

"We just think there are synergies which would benefit our operations. We would look at that (expanding) down the road. It's very early in the process, but we never say never," said John Hotard, a spokesman for American Airlines.

American expects a majority of the Shuttle's 600 employees would be retained, Hotard said. American said it has not decided whether the Shuttle would be operated by its mainline pilots or its American Eagle unit pilots.
If American succeeded in its bid to buy the Shuttle, competition would intensify for the Delta Shuttle, which operates in the same area, analysts said.
"American is a stronger competitor. It makes it a tougher market for Delta," Browning said.
AMR Corp.'s stock gained 62.5 cents to $97.50 a share in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. US Airways gained 12.5 cents to $34.75, also on the NYSE.
